items.stem: A nurse finishes a dressing change and is about to leave the unit for break. According to College of Nurses of Ontario documentation expectations and standard nursing documentation practice, which action is required?

options.text: Document the dressing change before providing the care so the record is ready.
Document the care at the time it is provided or as soon as possible afterward, including date and time.
Wait until the end of the week and write one summary note for all dressing changes.
Ask a colleague who did not provide the care to document the dressing change later.

rationales.A: Incorrect. CNO states nurses do not document before the care is provided.
rationales.B: Correct. CNO requires documentation in a timely manner at the time care is provided or as soon as possible afterward, with date and time; OpenStax emphasizes charting in real time to keep records accurate and current.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Delayed weekly summary charting does not meet timely, contemporaneous documentation expectations.
rationales.D: Incorrect. CNO directs nurses to document care they provide and not document care provided by another individual (except designated recorder situations).

items.topic: Documentation — timely; do not document before care
items.jurisdiction_note: CNO Documentation practice standard sets Ontario nursing documentation accountabilities; OpenStax supports real-time charting as general best practice.

sources.title: Documentation
sources.section: Accountabilities — timely documentation; do not document before care
sources.evidence: Document in a timely manner, either at the time they provide care or as soon as possible after; nurses do not document before the care is provided.

sources.title: 14.5 Guidelines for Effective Documentation
sources.evidence: Charting in real time is necessary for maintaining accurate and up-to-date patient records.

items.stem: A former inpatient sends a personal social media friend request to the nurse who provided care. Which response best maintains professional boundaries?

options.text: Accept the request and discuss the client’s hospital stay privately in direct messages.
Decline connecting on personal social media and maintain professional boundaries online.
Accept the request only if the client promises not to mention health information.
Accept the request because the therapeutic relationship ended at discharge, so boundaries no longer apply.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Discussing care on personal social media risks privacy breaches and blurs professional boundaries.
rationales.B: Correct. CNO directs nurses not to accept friend requests from clients on personal social media; NCSBN advises caution with online social contact because it blurs professional and personal relationships even if the patient initiates contact.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Conditional acceptance still creates an inappropriate personal online relationship.
rationales.D: Incorrect. NCSBN notes online contact with former patients also blurs professional and personal relationships; CNO requires maintaining boundaries.

items.topic: Professional boundaries — no personal social media connections with clients
items.jurisdiction_note: CNO Professional Boundaries is the Ontario regulator authority; NCSBN social media guidance independently supports avoiding personal online relationships with patients/former patients.

sources.title: Professional Boundaries and Nurse-Client Relationships
sources.section: Technology use / social media — refrain from friend requests
sources.evidence: Nurses must refrain from connecting with clients, following clients, or accepting friend requests from clients on their personal social media accounts.

sources.title: A Nurse's Guide to the Use of Social Media
sources.evidence: Use caution when having online social contact with patients or former patients; online contact blurs professional and personal relationships; patient initiation does not permit a personal relationship.

verification_log.by: AI author (Composer, Cursor subagent bc-6659b924) — not a licensed clinician
verification_log.checks: CNO no friend requests + NCSBN online contact blurs boundaries

items.stem: Under Ontario’s Health Care Consent Act and CNO Consent guidance, which statement about decision-making capacity is accurate?

options.text: A finding of incapacity for one treatment means the person is incapable for all treatments indefinitely.
A person may be incapable with respect to some treatments and capable with respect to others.
Only a court can ever determine that a person is capable of consenting to treatment.
Capacity is assessed once on admission and never reassessed during the hospital stay.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Capacity is treatment-specific; incapacity for one treatment does not automatically apply to all treatments.
rationales.B: Correct. HCCA s.15 and CNO Consent state a person may be capable for some treatments and incapable for others; capacity can also change over time.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Health practitioners assess capacity related to specific treatment decisions under the HCCA framework.
rationales.D: Incorrect. HCCA recognizes capacity may change with time; consent is an ongoing process.

items.jurisdiction_note: HCCA s.15 and CNO Consent are Ontario authorities for capacity assessment.

sources.title: Health Care Consent Act, 1996
sources.evidence: A person may be incapable with respect to some treatments and capable with respect to others; a person may be incapable at one time and capable at another.

sources.title: Consent
sources.section: HCCA — capacity relates to a specific treatment
sources.evidence: Consent to treatment, and assessing capacity to consent, must relate to a specific treatment or plan of treatment; a person could be capable for one treatment but incapable with respect to another.

verification_log.by: AI author (Composer, Cursor subagent bc-6659b924) — not a licensed clinician
verification_log.checks: HCCA s.15 + CNO Consent treatment-specific capacity

items.stem: A client becomes angry about a delayed procedure and raises their voice at the nurse. Which initial conflict-management action best aligns with College of Nurses of Ontario guidance?

options.text: Argue that the delay is not the nurse’s fault and criticize the client’s tone.
Remain calm, encourage the client to express concerns, and avoid arguing or judging.
Ignore the behaviour because conflict is never an issue nurses should address.
Immediately permanently discontinue all nursing services without assessing safety or planning alternatives.

rationales.A: Incorrect. CNO advises nurses to avoid arguing, criticizing, defending, or judging.
rationales.B: Correct. CNO conflict-management strategies include remaining calm, encouraging expression of concerns, and avoiding arguing/criticizing; OpenStax notes good communication promotes better handling of conflicts and emphasizes respectful, assertive professional communication.
rationales.C: Incorrect. CNO states unmanaged conflict can hinder care and escalate into violence/abuse; nurses must be prepared to prevent or manage conflict.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Withdrawal of services is a last-resort safety option with decision-tree guidance, not the first response to voiced frustration.

items.topic: Conflict prevention and management — calm, non-argumentative response
items.jurisdiction_note: CNO Conflict Prevention and Management is the Ontario practice guideline; OpenStax supports communication skills that help manage conflict.

sources.title: Conflict Prevention and Management
sources.evidence: Remain calm and encourage the client to express concerns; avoid arguing, criticizing, defending or judging.

sources.title: 2.3 Effective Communication
sources.evidence: Good communication among healthcare providers also promotes better handling of conflicts; professional communication includes courtesy, empathy, and assertiveness.

verification_log.checks: CNO conflict remain calm/avoid arguing + OpenStax communication/conflict

items.stem: Which documentation practices meet College of Nurses of Ontario accountabilities? Select all that apply.

options.text: Include the date and time with documentation entries.
Document care before it is provided to save time.
Clearly identify a late entry and refer to the date and time the care occurred.
Falsify a record if asked by a colleague to “fix” a missed note.
Document in a timely manner at or soon after the care or event.

rationales.A: Correct. CNO requires all documentation entries include the date and time; OpenStax notes entries need an accurate date and time stamp.
rationales.B: Incorrect. CNO states nurses do not document before care is provided.
rationales.C: Correct. CNO requires late entries to be indicated with the date/time the care or action occurred.
rationales.D: Incorrect. CNO prohibits falsifying a record relating to practice.
rationales.E: Correct. CNO requires timely documentation at the time of care or as soon as possible afterward; OpenStax supports real-time charting.

items.topic: Documentation accountabilities SATA — date/time, timely, late entry, no falsify
items.jurisdiction_note: CNO Documentation is Ontario regulator authority; OpenStax supports date/time stamp and timely documentation principles.

sources.title: Documentation
sources.section: Accountabilities — date/time, timely, late entry, no falsify
sources.evidence: Ensure entries include date and time; document timely; indicate a late entry; do not falsify a record; do not document before care.

sources.title: 14.5 Guidelines for Effective Documentation
sources.section: ANA documentation principles; Chart in Real Time
sources.evidence: Each documented entry must be authenticated with an accurate date and time stamp; charting in real time maintains accurate, up-to-date records.

items.stem: According to Ontario’s Health Care Consent Act definition of capacity (also reflected in CNO Consent guidance), a person is capable with respect to a treatment if the person is able to:

options.text: Recite the hospital mission statement from memory.
Understand relevant information and appreciate the reasonably foreseeable consequences of a decision or lack of decision.
Name three nurses on the unit and state their years of experience.
Sign any form placed in front of them, regardless of understanding.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Capacity concerns decision-relevant treatment information, not institutional trivia.
rationales.B: Correct. HCCA s.4 and CNO Consent define capacity as ability to understand relevant information and appreciate reasonably foreseeable consequences of a decision or lack of decision.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Naming staff is unrelated to treatment decision-making capacity.
rationales.D: Incorrect. A signature without understanding does not constitute capable informed consent.

items.topic: Capacity definition — understand and appreciate consequences
items.jurisdiction_note: HCCA s.4 capacity definition is Ontario statute; CNO Consent restates the understand/appreciate test for nurses.

sources.title: Health Care Consent Act, 1996
sources.evidence: A person is capable if able to understand information relevant to making a decision and able to appreciate the reasonably foreseeable consequences of a decision or lack of decision.

sources.title: Consent
sources.evidence: Capable if understands information relevant to making a decision concerning treatment and appreciates the reasonably possible consequences of a decision or lack of a decision.

verification_log.checks: HCCA s.4 + CNO Consent understand/appreciate capacity definition

items.stem: Fifteen minutes after a packed red blood cell transfusion is started, the client develops chills, fever, and low back pain. Which action should the nurse take FIRST?

options.text: Slow the transfusion rate and reassess in 30 minutes.
Stop the transfusion immediately and keep the IV line open with normal saline.
Administer prescribed acetaminophen and continue the same unit at the previous rate.
Complete the remaining unit quickly so the reaction can be evaluated afterward.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Suspected transfusion reactions require immediate stop, not merely slowing the infusion.
rationales.B: Correct. Merck directs stopping the transfusion immediately and keeping the IV open with normal saline; OpenStax likewise prioritizes immediately stopping the transfusion when a reaction is occurring.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Continuing the same unit after systemic reaction symptoms is unsafe; the unit should not be restarted.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Completing the unit would increase exposure to the implicated product.

sources.title: Complications of Transfusion
sources.evidence: If reaction symptoms occur (other than localized urticaria/itching), the transfusion should be stopped immediately and the IV line kept open with normal saline; the unit should not be restarted.

sources.title: 16.7 Blood Products and Transfusion Principles
sources.section: Prioritizing Hypotheses, Generating Solutions, and Taking Action
sources.evidence: Immediately stopping the blood transfusion when a reaction is occurring is important; Stop the transfusion.

verification_log.by: AI author (Composer, Cursor subagent bc-6659b924) — not a licensed clinician
verification_log.checks: Merck stop transfusion + NS open; OpenStax stop transfusion first

items.stem: A nurse is teaching a client newly started on warfarin. Which instruction is the priority safety teaching point?

options.text: Stop all follow-up blood tests once you feel well.
Report signs and symptoms of bleeding and keep scheduled INR monitoring appointments.
Double the next dose if a dose is missed, without contacting the prescriber.
Take an extra aspirin daily to enhance warfarin’s effect.

rationales.A: Incorrect. DailyMed requires regular INR monitoring in all treated patients.
rationales.B: Correct. DailyMed boxed warning instructs patients about prevention measures and to report bleeding signs/symptoms, with regular INR monitoring; Merck notes warfarin requires close INR monitoring and carries bleeding risk.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Missed-dose management should follow prescriber/label guidance; doubling without advice increases bleeding risk.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Combining with antiplatelet agents can increase bleeding risk and is not routine teaching.

items.jurisdiction_note: DailyMed is a US FDA label source; bleeding risk and INR monitoring teaching is concordant with Canadian warfarin practice.

sources.title: WARFARIN SODIUM tablet
sources.publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine — DailyMed
sources.evidence: Warfarin can cause major or fatal bleeding; perform regular INR monitoring; instruct patients about prevention measures to minimize bleeding risk and to report signs and symptoms of bleeding.

sources.title: Deep Venous Thrombosis (DVT)
sources.section: Anticoagulation strategies — warfarin INR monitoring; bleeding
sources.evidence: Warfarin with close INR monitoring; compared with DOACs, warfarin requires ongoing laboratory testing and has serious bleeding risk considerations.

verification_log.checks: DailyMed warfarin bleeding/INR teaching + Merck DVT warfarin INR monitoring

items.stem: A client is receiving IV gentamicin. Which adverse effects should the nurse monitor for most closely because of aminoglycoside toxicity?

options.text: Nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity (vestibular/auditory).
Only mild transient hair loss without other risks.
Hyperglycemia as the primary expected effect.
Permanent blue-green skin discoloration in all clients.

rationales.A: Correct. Merck states all aminoglycosides cause renal toxicity and vestibular/auditory toxicity; DailyMed gentamicin boxed warning highlights nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity (vestibular and auditory).
rationales.B: Incorrect. Hair loss is not the primary boxed aminoglycoside toxicity concern.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Hyperglycemia is not the hallmark aminoglycoside toxicity described in these sources.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Not a described primary toxicity of gentamicin/aminoglycosides in the cited sources.

sources.title: Aminoglycosides
sources.evidence: All aminoglycosides cause renal toxicity (often reversible) and vestibular and auditory toxicity (often irreversible).

sources.title: GENTAMICIN sulfate injection
sources.publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine — DailyMed
sources.evidence: Gentamicin is potentially nephrotoxic; neurotoxicity manifested by ototoxicity, both vestibular and auditory, can occur.

verification_log.checks: Merck aminoglycoside renal/oto toxicity + DailyMed gentamicin boxed warning

items.stem: A client is admitted with suspected chickenpox (varicella) and active vesicular lesions. Which transmission-based precautions are indicated?

options.text: Standard Precautions only; no room placement considerations.
Airborne Precautions plus Contact Precautions (with Standard Precautions).
Droplet Precautions alone without airborne controls.
Protective (neutropenic) precautions only, without isolation of the infectious client.

rationales.A: Incorrect. CDC lists varicella as Airborne + Contact + Standard, not Standard alone.
rationales.B: Correct. CDC Appendix A specifies Airborne + Contact + Standard for varicella until lesions are dry and crusted; Merck describes spread by infected airborne droplets/aerosolized particles and by direct contact with virus from skin lesions.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Droplet alone is insufficient for varicella; airborne controls are required.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Protective precautions protect immunocompromised hosts; the infectious varicella client needs source isolation.

items.client_needs_subcategory: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control

sources.title: Isolation Precautions Appendix A — Type and Duration
sources.publisher: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
sources.evidence: Varicella Zoster: Airborne + Contact + Standard until lesions dry and crusted.

sources.title: Chickenpox (Varicella)
sources.evidence: Spread by mucosal inoculation via infected airborne droplets or aerosolized particles and by direct contact with the virus (eg, via skin lesions).

items.stem: A client is diagnosed with pertussis (whooping cough). Which precautions should the nurse implement?

options.text: Airborne Precautions with an airborne infection isolation room as first-line for all cases.
Droplet Precautions (with Standard Precautions), continued per guidance until effective antibiotic therapy criteria are met.
Contact Precautions only, because pertussis is spread solely by fomites.
No precautions are needed after the first hour of hospitalization.

rationales.A: Incorrect. CDC lists pertussis under Droplet Precautions, not Airborne.
rationales.B: Correct. CDC specifies Droplet + Standard for pertussis until 5 days after initiation of effective antibiotic therapy; Merck notes droplet transmission and recommends respiratory droplet isolation until antibiotics have been given for 5 days.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Merck states transmission by contaminated articles is rare; primary spread is respiratory droplets.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Isolation continues for the CDC/Merck antibiotic-duration window, not one hour.

sources.title: Isolation Precautions Appendix A — Type and Duration
sources.publisher: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
sources.evidence: Pertussis: Droplet + Standard until 5 days after initiation of effective antibiotic therapy.

sources.title: Pertussis (Whooping Cough)
sources.evidence: Transmission mainly via droplets of respiratory secretions; hospitalization with respiratory droplet isolation until antibiotics have been given for 5 days.

items.stem: A postoperative client after thyroid surgery has perioral tingling and a positive Chvostek sign. Which electrolyte imbalance should the nurse suspect?

options.text: Hypernatremia
Hypocalcemia
Hypermagnesemia as the only explanation
Isolated hyperchloremia without calcium change

rationales.A: Incorrect. Hypernatremia presents with thirst/neurologic changes, not Chvostek sign as the classic bedside cue.
rationales.B: Correct. Merck identifies Chvostek and Trousseau signs for latent tetany of hypocalcemia; OpenStax lists positive Chvostek’s and Trousseau’s signs among hypocalcemia manifestations, including paresthesia around the lips.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Hypermagnesemia is not the classic association for Chvostek sign in these sources.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Chloride imbalance is not linked to Chvostek sign in the cited sources.

sources.title: Hypocalcemia
sources.evidence: Chvostek and Trousseau signs are easily elicited to identify latent tetany; tetany includes paresthesias of the lips, tongue, fingers, and feet.

sources.title: 10.3 Electrolyte Imbalance
sources.evidence: Hypocalcemia manifestations include paresthesia (especially around the lips, tongue, hands, and feet) and positive Chvostek’s and Trousseau’s signs.

verification_log.checks: Merck Chvostek/Trousseau hypocalcemia; OpenStax same cues

items.units_note: Potassium mmol/L = mEq/L. Reference interval varies by laboratory.
items.stem: A client taking a loop diuretic reports new muscle weakness and polyuria. Serum potassium is 2.8 mmol/L. Which interpretation is most accurate?

options.text: Findings are consistent with hypokalemia, which can cause muscle weakness and cardiac effects.
Hypokalemia never affects skeletal muscle or the heart.
A potassium of 2.8 mmol/L is above the usual reference interval and indicates hyperkalemia.
Polyuria rules out any potassium imbalance.

rationales.A: Correct. Merck lists muscle weakness and polyuria among hypokalemia features and notes cardiac hyperexcitability with severe hypokalemia; OpenStax lists muscle weakness/cramps and ECG changes among hypokalemia manifestations, with serum potassium <3.5 mEq/L.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Both sources describe neuromuscular and cardiac effects of hypokalemia.
rationales.C: Incorrect. 2.8 mmol/L is below the usual ~3.5 mmol/L threshold cited for hypokalemia.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Merck includes polyuria among hypokalemia clinical features.

items.topic: Hypokalemia — muscle weakness and cardiac risk

sources.title: Hypokalemia
sources.evidence: Hypokalemia is serum potassium <3.5 mEq/L (<3.5 mmol/L); clinical features include muscle weakness and polyuria; cardiac hyperexcitability may occur with severe hypokalemia.

sources.title: 10.3 Electrolyte Imbalance
sources.evidence: Hypokalemia manifestations include muscle weakness or cramps; serum potassium level (<3.5 mEq/L); both types of potassium imbalance can cause cardiac dysrhythmias.
